title: Why America’s Only Private Intercity Railroad Just Went Bankrupt
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
On September 24th, 2026, 17 companies most people had never heard of walked into a bankruptcy court in New Jersey, owing about $2.5 billion. The next morning, a bright yellow Brightline train left Miami on time, accelerated to 125 mph toward Orlando, and was nearly full. That September, Brightline carried 267,765 passengers, 18% more than a year earlier.

So how can America's only privately funded intercity railroad have busier trains every month and bankrupt owners at the same time?

This video starts with why nobody in America had built a private passenger railroad in more than a century, and why Wes Edens and Fortress thought Florida could change that. It then follows the money: a $6 billion Orlando extension financed largely with tax-exempt municipal bonds, projections of 8 million riders and $600 million in ticket revenue, and the reality of 3.1 million riders and $214 million. It also covers cheaper fares, 10–11% interest rates, a five-notch downgrade to CCC, two failed rescue searches, and a bankruptcy designed so the trains never stop. Finally, it asks what this means for Brightline West, the $21 billion high-speed line planned between Las Vegas and Los Angeles.

title: Why It's Cheaper to Sometimes Sink a Ship than Fix It
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Once you stop thinking of a ship as a vehicle and start thinking of it as a spreadsheet, the answer is simple. This video looks at how a ship's value falls every year until it hits its scrap-steel floor. It covers why owners sell ships for scrap just before their fourth or fifth special survey, and how insurers decide a ship is a "constructive total loss". We also go through the Salem, a supertanker sunk in one of the biggest marine insurance frauds in history, and why removing the Costa Concordia cost almost three times what it took to build. Then there are the ships sunk on purpose, completely legally: artificial reefs like the USS Oriskany, and warships used as SINKEX targets. Last stop is the beaches of Alang, Chittagong and Gadani, where most of the world's old ships end up.

A ship is never worth what it cost to build. It's worth only what it can earn on its next voyage.

title: Why BYD is Buying Ships
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
In January 2024, BYD Explorer No. 1 left Shenzhen carrying about 5,000 electric cars. A carmaker owning the ships that carry its cars used to make no sense: carmakers built cars and shipping lines moved them. Then BYD ran out of ships to rent.

This video explains:

The ships: how pure car and truck carriers work, the “floating shoeboxes” that hold about 6,500–7,000 cars each.
The fleet: why only about 800 large car carriers exist.
The squeeze: how the pandemic and China’s export boom used up that fleet.
The cost: charter rates went from about $10,000 a day in 2020 to about $115,000 a day by late 2023. On a China–Brazil round trip, that’s close to $1,000 per car just to rent the ship.
BYD’s answer:
an 8-ship fleet led by the 9,200-car BYD Shenzhen, which briefly beat Höegh Aurora as the largest car carrier ever built
10 more ships ordered from three Chinese shipyards
a planned fleet of 18 ships with more than 130,000 car spaces
Other Chinese carmakers: SAIC Anji, Chery and Foton–COSCO are building fleets too, including a combined order for up to 21 ultra-large carriers.
The shipyards: China now builds most of the new car carriers, makes most of the cargo, and increasingly owns the ships in between.
The pushback: Europe’s EV tariffs and the US port fee of $46 per net ton.
The risk: the fleet heads toward 1,000 car carriers by 2030, and shipping booms usually end in a bust.

For a century, cars followed ships. Now the ships follow the cars.
